items.stem: Explain how bid-rent theory accounts for the pattern of land use in a city.
items.answer: Accessibility is greatest at the centre, so land values are highest; retail and offices can pay the most for central sites; industry and high-density housing outbid others further out; low-density housing and agriculture occupy the edge.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point [4]

items.stem: Explain the limitations of the Burgess model for modern cities.
items.answer: Based on 1920s Chicago; ignores relief, transport routes and planning; car ownership and out-of-town retail; decentralisation and multiple centres; gentrification; LIC cities differ.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per limitation [3]

items.answer: For: Models are based on historical cities (Chicago 1920s-30s); decentralisation, edge cities, gentrification and globalisation have changed patterns. items.stem: To what extent do you agree that managing transport is the most important challenge in creating sustainable cities? In your answer you may refer to housing and equity.
items.answer: For: Transport affects air quality, emissions, congestion, access to jobs and land use; BRT (Curitiba, Bogotá), road pricing (London, Singapore). items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “In LIC cities, wealthy people often live near the centre.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) A student writes: “Urban models describe every city exactly.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Elite residential areas lie close to the CBD and along a spine, with informal settlements on the edge (Griffin-Ford). (b) Not correct. Models are simplifications; real cities are affected by relief, history, planning and transport.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain the limitations of the Burgess model for modern cities. (b) A revision website states: “Land values always fall evenly in all directions from the CBD.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Based on 1920s Chicago; ignores relief, transport routes and planning; car ownership and out-of-town retail; decentralisation and multiple centres; gentrification; LIC cities differ. (b) Not correct. Secondary peaks occur at suburban centres and along main roads and rail lines.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per limitation [3] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.answer: Secondary centres and out-of-town retail; transport routes create sectors; planning controls; relief and rivers; historical land uses.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Fig. 18.1 is based on bid-rent theory. The rent (US$ per m² per year) each land use is willing to pay falls with distance d (km) from the CBD: retail: 1149 − 324d; offices and industry: 695 − 113d; housing: 292 − 31d. (a) Calculate the distance at which housing outbids offices and industry. (b) Explain why retail can pay the highest rents near the CBD.
items.answer: (a) 4.91 km (b) The centre is the most accessible point, so shops attract the most customers (high threshold and range) and make high profits; they need little space.

items.stem: “Models of urban structure are no longer useful for understanding modern cities.” How far do you agree with this statement? In your answer you may refer to decentralisation and bid-rent theory.
items.answer: For: Models are based on historical cities (Chicago 1920s-30s); decentralisation, edge cities, gentrification and globalisation have changed patterns. Against: They provide a framework for comparison, explain processes (bid-rent, filtering, invasion and succession), and modified models (Griffin-Ford, multiple nuclei) describe modern and LIC cities. Conclusion: Models remain useful as simplified frameworks for explaining processes, provided their assumptions and limitations are recognised.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “previously developed land that has become vacant or derelict”.
items.answer: Brownfield site
items.markingKey: Brownfield site: previously developed land that has become vacant or derelict. [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “Brownfield redevelopment helps protect green belts.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain the causes of gentrification.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Reusing urban land reduces pressure to build on greenfield sites. (b) Young professionals attracted by cheap, well-built older housing near city-centre jobs and amenities; changing lifestyles; investment by developers; regeneration policies; rising suburban costs and commuting times.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark per cause [3]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why retailing has decentralised from CBDs. (b) Explain how CBDs have responded to retail decline.
items.answer: (a) Car ownership; cheaper land and free parking at the edge; congestion and high rents in the CBD; large stores need space; suburbanisation of customers; online shopping. (b) Pedestrianisation, improved public transport, leisure and food uses, events, conversions to housing, business improvement districts, covered shopping centres.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per reason [4] (b) [3]

items.stem: In an inner suburb of Melbourne, the mean house price rose from 174 000 to 387 000 (local currency units) over 20 years, while the percentage of residents in professional and managerial jobs rose from 14% to 41%. (a) Calculate the mean annual (compound) rate of increase in house prices. (b) Explain the possible effects of these changes on long-term residents.
items.answer: (a) 4.08% per year (b) Rising rents and property taxes force out low-income tenants; loss of local shops and community ties; but owners gain from higher values and the environment improves.

items.stem: In an old district of Lisbon, the mean house price rose from 216 000 to 690 000 (local currency units) over 15 years, while the percentage of residents in professional and managerial jobs rose from 18% to 39%. (a) Calculate the mean annual (compound) rate of increase in house prices. (b) Explain how the data provide evidence of gentrification.
items.answer: (a) 8.05% per year (b) Rapidly rising house prices together with a growing share of professional workers show higher-income groups moving in.

items.stem: Tomás argues that gentrification brings more benefits than costs to urban areas. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples.
items.answer: For: Improved housing and environment, new businesses and jobs, higher local tax revenue, reduced crime (Islington, Brooklyn). Against: Displacement of lower-income residents and long-established businesses; loss of community and identity; rising rents; social polarisation. Conclusion: Gentrification improves the physical environment but the benefits mostly go to newcomers; policies such as rent control and affordable housing are needed for wider benefit.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “bus rapid transit (BRT)”?
options: A high-capacity bus system with dedicated lanes and stations, such as in Curitiba or Bogotá.
A fee charged to drive into a defined central area at busy times.
The percentage of journeys made by each form of transport.
A city with high-density, mixed-use development that reduces travel distances.
items.answer: A high-capacity bus system with dedicated lanes and stations, such as in Curitiba or Bogotá.
items.markingKey: Bus rapid transit (BRT): a high-capacity bus system with dedicated lanes and stations, such as in Curitiba or Bogotá. [1]

items.stem: A revision website states: “Sustainable urban management only concerns the environment.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. It also covers social equity and economic viability.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain the challenges of providing housing in rapidly growing LIC cities. (b) A student writes: “Building more roads permanently solves congestion.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Rapid population growth; low incomes; high land prices; lack of finance; informal land markets; limited infrastructure. (b) Not correct. New roads often generate extra traffic (induced demand).
items.markingKey: (a) [3] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Table 18.3 shows the modal split (% of journeys) in Bogotá before and ten years after a new transport strategy: car: 36% to 30%; bus or BRT: 13% to 18%; rail or metro: 6% to 7%; cycling: 2% to 3%; walking: 43% to 42%. If there are 4 million journeys a day, calculate the reduction in daily car journeys.
items.answer: 0.24 million

items.stem: Table 18.3 shows the modal split (% of journeys) in London before and ten years after a new transport strategy: car: 41% to 30%; bus or BRT: 15% to 26%; rail or metro: 5% to 5%; cycling: 1% to 5%; walking: 38% to 34%. (a) Calculate the percentage of journeys made by sustainable modes (all except car) before and after. (b) If there are 8 million journeys a day, calculate the reduction in daily car journeys.
items.answer: (a) 59% to 70% (b) 0.88 million
items.markingKey: (a) sum of non-car modes [2] (b) 8 × (41 − 30)% [2]

items.stem: “Managing transport is the most important challenge in creating sustainable cities.” How far do you agree with this statement? In your answer you may refer to public transport and energy.
items.answer: For: Transport affects air quality, emissions, congestion, access to jobs and land use; BRT (Curitiba, Bogotá), road pricing (London, Singapore). Against: Housing (informal settlements, affordability), water and sanitation, waste, energy and social equity are equally or more pressing, especially in LIC cities. Conclusion: Transport is central because it shapes urban form, but sustainability requires integrated management of housing, services and energy.
